lessons.summary: Use particle structure and electron arrangement to explain isotopes, ions and periodic behaviour.
objectives: Relate atomic and mass numbers to particles.
Represent ions and isotopes.
Use electron arrangement to explain chemical behaviour.
keyIdeas: Atomic number equals proton number.
Isotopes share proton number but differ in neutron number.
Ions form when electrons are gained or lost.

definitions.meaning: Atoms of one element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers.
A charged particle formed when electrons are gained or lost.
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus.

method: Read atomic and mass numbers carefully.
Calculate neutrons as mass number minus atomic number.
Adjust electron count using the ion charge.
Link outer electrons to likely chemical behaviour.

workedExample.prompt: Describe the particles in a magnesium-24 ion, Mg²⁺, atomic number 12.
steps: Protons = 12.
Neutrons = 24 - 12 = 12.
A 2+ ion has lost two electrons, so electrons = 10.
workedExample.conclusion: Mg²⁺ contains 12 protons, 12 neutrons and 10 electrons.

misconceptions.mistake: Changing proton number when an ion forms.
misconceptions.correction: Chemical ion formation changes electrons; changing protons changes the element.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating relative atomic mass as the mass number of every atom.
misconceptions.correction: Relative atomic mass is a weighted mean across naturally occurring isotopes.

practice.prompt: An atom has atomic number 17 and mass number 35. Determine its protons, neutrons and electrons.
hints: A neutral atom has equal protons and electrons.
solution: 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 17 electrons.
successCriteria: Neutron calculation uses mass number minus atomic number

practice.prompt: Explain why chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 have similar chemical behaviour.
hints: Focus on electrons, not neutrons.
solution: Both isotopes have atomic number 17.
Neutral atoms therefore have the same electron arrangement.
Chemical reactions depend mainly on outer electrons, so their behaviour is similar.

practice.prompt: A sample contains 75% isotope X-10 and 25% isotope X-11. Calculate the relative atomic mass.
hints: Use a weighted mean.

practice.prompt: Oxygen-18 has atomic number 8. Determine the particle counts in an O²⁻ ion.
hints: Subtract atomic number from mass number.
A negative charge means extra electrons.
solution: There are 8 protons and 18 − 8 = 10 neutrons.
A 2− charge gives 8 + 2 = 10 electrons.

practice.prompt: An element sample contains 80% Y-24 and 20% Y-26. Calculate its relative atomic mass and explain whether every atom has that mass number.
hints: Use fractional weights.
A mean need not equal either isotope mass.
solution: Individual atoms have mass numbers 24 or 26; 24.4 is the sample average.
successCriteria: Distinguishes average from individual mass number.

checklist: I calculate particle counts from isotope notation.
I explain ion charge using electrons.
I distinguish mass number from relative atomic mass.
I connect outer electrons to reactions.

notes.title: From isotope abundance to average mass
paragraphs: An ion’s charge compares proton and electron counts; neutrons do not contribute to the net electrical charge. A negative ion has more electrons than protons. Isotope notation identifies the proton number and total nucleon number, so neutron count follows by subtraction. An element sample may contain several isotopes, and its relative atomic mass is their abundance-weighted mean. That mean can be non-integer even though each individual nucleus contains whole numbers of particles. In school calculations, use the supplied isotope masses and fractions rather than rounding the mean to a mass number.

workedExamples.prompt: A sample has 60% X-20 and 40% X-22. All X atoms have atomic number 10. Find relative atomic mass and neutrons in each isotope.
steps: Neutron counts are 20 − 10 = 10 and 22 − 10 = 12.
workedExamples.conclusion: Relative atomic mass 20.8 describes the sample average, not an individual nucleus.

flashcards.front: How many extra electrons does a 2− ion have?
flashcards.back: Two more electrons than protons.

flashcards.front: What changes between isotopes of one element?
flashcards.back: Neutron number.

flashcards.front: Why can relative atomic mass be non-integer?
flashcards.back: It is an abundance-weighted average.

flashcards.front: What does mass number count?
flashcards.back: Protons plus neutrons in one nucleus.

diagrams.title: From isotope abundance to average mass
diagrams.description: The contributions are combined rather than selecting the commonest mass.

lessons.summary: Use electrostatic models to connect particle structure with material properties.
objectives: Compare ionic, covalent and metallic models.
Represent electron transfer or sharing.
Explain properties from structure.
keyIdeas: Bonding models explain attractions between charged particles.
Structure extends beyond one bond to a lattice or molecule.
Property explanations need particles, attraction and mobility.

definitions.meaning: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Attraction between shared electrons and two nuclei.
An electron able to move through a larger structure rather than belonging to one atom.

method: Identify the particles present.
Describe charge or electron behaviour.
Describe the larger structure.
Link an applied condition to particle movement or attraction.

workedExample.prompt: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct but molten sodium chloride does.
steps: Both states contain charged ions.
In the solid lattice, ions vibrate but cannot move through the material.
When molten, ions are mobile and carry charge.
workedExample.conclusion: Conductivity changes because charge carriers become mobile, not because new ions appear.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling every strong substance a molecule.
misconceptions.correction: Ionic and metallic solids are extended lattices rather than discrete molecules.

misconceptions.mistake: Saying bonds break when a molecular substance melts.
misconceptions.correction: Melting usually overcomes intermolecular attractions, not covalent bonds inside molecules.

practice.prompt: Describe the electron change when magnesium forms Mg²⁺.
hints: Use magnesium outer electrons.
solution: A magnesium atom loses two electrons.
It then has two more protons than electrons and charge 2+.

practice.prompt: Explain why metals conduct electricity as solids.
hints: Name the mobile particles.
solution: Metallic structures contain positive ions and delocalised electrons.
The electrons can move through the lattice.
Their movement transfers charge.

practice.prompt: Compare the melting behaviour of a simple molecular substance and a giant covalent substance.
hints: Distinguish attractions between molecules from covalent networks.
solution: A simple molecular solid melts when relatively weak intermolecular attractions are overcome.
A giant covalent structure requires many strong covalent bonds to be overcome.
It therefore generally has a much higher melting temperature.

practice.prompt: A simple molecular solid melts without decomposing. Explain what changes and what remains intact in its particles.
hints: Distinguish within-molecule bonds from between-molecule attractions.
Melting is a change of state.
solution: Molecules become able to move past each other as some intermolecular attractions are overcome.
The molecules retain their internal covalent bonds because no decomposition occurs.

practice.prompt: Compare charge carriers in molten sodium chloride and solid copper.
hints: Name the mobile charged entities in each.
Do not call ions electrons.
solution: Molten sodium chloride conducts through mobile positive and negative ions.
Copper conducts through mobile delocalised electrons while its positive ion lattice remains in place.
successCriteria: Distinguishes lattice motion from charge motion.

checklist: I distinguish bonds from intermolecular attractions.
I connect structure to observed properties.

notes.title: Graphite links structure to two properties
paragraphs: Carbon shows why naming an element is insufficient to predict a material’s properties. In diamond, each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds in a three-dimensional network. Graphite has strong covalent bonds within layers and much weaker attractions between layers. One electron per carbon contributes to delocalised electrons within the layered structure, enabling electrical conduction. Sliding layers explain graphite’s softness without suggesting that all its bonds are weak. A property explanation should identify both the arrangement and the relevant interaction or mobile particle; the word strong alone does not identify the mechanism.

workedExamples.prompt: Explain how graphite can conduct electricity yet feel soft, using its structure.
steps: Delocalised electrons can move through the layered structure and carry charge.
Layers can slide because attractions between them are weaker than the covalent bonds within each layer.
workedExamples.conclusion: Conductivity and softness arise from different structural features.

flashcards.front: Why does diamond resist deformation?
flashcards.back: Its extended three-dimensional covalent network is rigid.

flashcards.front: What carries charge in graphite?
flashcards.back: Delocalised electrons.

flashcards.front: Are graphite’s in-layer bonds weak?
flashcards.back: No; the covalent bonds within layers are strong.

flashcards.front: What explains graphite layers sliding?
flashcards.back: Relatively weak attractions between layers.

diagrams.title: Graphite links structure to two properties
diagrams.description: Different structural features explain conduction and softness.

nodes.label: Covalent sheets
nodes.detail: Strong bonds join carbon atoms within each layer

nodes.label: Weak interlayer attraction
nodes.detail: Sheets can slide; graphite is soft

edges.label: contrast charge movement with layer movement

lessons.summary: Use electron arrangement to explain recurring properties and qualify simple trends in the periodic table.
objectives: Relate periods and groups to electron arrangement.
Explain selected radius and reactivity trends.
Distinguish a useful pattern from an exceptionless rule.
explanation: Elements are ordered by increasing proton number. Their recurring chemical properties are connected to outer electron arrangements. In a simple shell model for the first twenty elements, the period indicates the occupied shell count. Main-group elements in the same group have similar outer arrangements, which helps explain similar ion formation and reactions; helium needs separate treatment because its first shell is full with two electrons.

Across a typical main-group period, increasing nuclear charge tends to pull electrons in the same main shell closer, so atomic radius generally decreases. Down a group, additional shells and shielding generally increase radius. Reactivity is not one universal left-to-right scale: losing an electron and gaining one depend differently on these factors, and the trend must be tied to the particular group and reaction.
keyIdeas: Proton number determines table order.
Outer electrons help explain chemical similarity.
A trend needs a named property and a defined comparison.

definitions.meaning: A horizontal row of the periodic table.
A vertical column whose main-group elements have related outer electron arrangements.
Reduction of the nuclear attraction experienced by an electron due to other electrons.

method: Identify the element’s proton number and electron arrangement.
Locate its period and group using the relevant table convention.
Compare shell count, nuclear charge and shielding.
Connect those factors to the named property without claiming a universal reactivity rule.

workedExample.prompt: Compare sodium (2,8,1) and potassium (2,8,8,1) using a simple shell model. Explain why potassium generally loses its outer electron more readily.
steps: Both have one outer electron, placing them in the same main group.
Potassium’s outer electron occupies an additional shell and experiences more shielding.
The greater distance and shielding outweigh the increased nuclear charge for this comparison.
workedExample.conclusion: Potassium generally loses its outer electron more readily. This explanation concerns electron loss in this group, not a universal rule that every larger atom is more reactive.

misconceptions.mistake: Saying elements in a group have the same number of total electrons.
misconceptions.correction: Their outer arrangements are related; total electron numbers differ.

misconceptions.mistake: Using one reactivity trend for every element.
misconceptions.correction: Name the group and the reaction or electron change being compared.

practice.prompt: An atom has electron arrangement 2,8,7. State its occupied shell count and outer electron count.
hints: Read each shell separately.
solution: It has three occupied shells and seven outer electrons.
In this simple model it belongs to period 3.

practice.prompt: Explain why a typical main-group atom tends to become smaller across a period even though more electrons are added.
hints: The added electrons enter the same main shell.
solution: Proton number and nuclear charge increase.
Added electrons occupy the same main shell, so shielding does not cancel the increased attraction.
The outer electron cloud is generally pulled closer; this is a trend rather than an exact rule for every radius definition.

practice.prompt: A learner says potassium must attract an extra electron more strongly than sodium because it has more protons. Evaluate the reasoning without making an unsupported prediction about a particular reaction.
hints: What else changes down the group?
solution: The argument considers nuclear charge but ignores additional shells, electron distance and shielding.
A prediction needs the relevant energy change and reaction context, not proton count alone.
The simple group trend for losing an outer electron cannot automatically be substituted for a claim about gaining one.

practice.prompt: An atom has shell arrangement 2,8,2. State its period and predict its common simple ion charge.
hints: Count occupied shells.
Consider losing the two outer electrons.
solution: Three occupied shells place it in period 3.
Loss of two electrons leaves a filled shell and a 2+ ion in the simple model.

practice.prompt: Why does more nuclear charge alone fail to predict the attraction on the outer electron when comparing atoms down a group?
hints: Consider both distance and intervening electrons.
Several factors change simultaneously.
solution: Extra shells place the outer electron farther from the nucleus and increase shielding.
These effects must be considered alongside nuclear charge, so proton count alone is insufficient.

checklist: I distinguish total and outer electrons.

notes.title: Separate period from outer-shell pattern
paragraphs: Main-group patterns connect shell structure to chemical behaviour, but individual properties require their own explanations. Across a period, proton number rises while outer electrons enter the same principal shell. Down a group, additional occupied shells increase the distance of outer electrons and the shielding by inner electrons. Noble gases have filled outer shells in the simple school model, which helps explain their low reactivity under ordinary conditions. Low reactivity is a qualified observation, not proof that an element can never form compounds. Electron arrangement is a model for explaining trends rather than a substitute for measured evidence.

workedExamples.prompt: Compare lithium, 2,1, with neon, 2,8, in the simple shell model.
steps: Both have two occupied shells, placing them in period 2.
Lithium has one outer electron; neon has a filled outer shell.
workedExamples.conclusion: Their different outer arrangements help explain contrasting ordinary chemical reactivity.

flashcards.front: What determines an element’s atomic number?
flashcards.back: Its proton count.

flashcards.front: What do occupied shells indicate in the simple main-group model?
flashcards.back: The period.

flashcards.front: Why are noble gases usually unreactive?
flashcards.back: Their outer shells are filled in the school model.

flashcards.front: What increases down a main group?
flashcards.back: Occupied shell count and generally shielding of outer electrons.

diagrams.title: Separate period from outer-shell pattern
diagrams.description: Two elements can share shell count without sharing outer electron arrangement.

lessons.summary: Represent chemical change with balanced equations while distinguishing evidence of a reaction from its explanation.
objectives: Conserve each element when balancing an equation.
Distinguish coefficients from formula subscripts.
Explain apparent mass changes using system boundaries.
explanation: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms into new combinations. The atoms of each element are conserved in an ordinary chemical reaction, so an equation needs the same count on both sides. A coefficient multiplies an entire formula. Changing a subscript changes the substance itself and is not a legitimate way to balance a fixed reaction.

Bubbles, a colour change or a temperature change may be evidence of a reaction, but each observation needs context. Bubbles can also arise from boiling or released dissolved gas. Conservation of mass applies to a closed system that retains all matter; an open container can appear to lose mass when gas leaves or gain mass when matter enters from the surroundings. Explain the boundary before declaring a conservation law broken.
keyIdeas: Equations conserve atoms rather than molecule counts.
Coefficients change amounts; subscripts identify composition.
Observations support an explanation but do not uniquely prove it.

definitions.meaning: A substance consumed in the chemical change being represented.
A substance formed in the chemical change being represented.
A number before a formula that multiplies every atom count in that formula.

method: Write correct formulas before balancing.
Count every element on both sides.
Adjust coefficients and simplify to the smallest whole-number ratio.
Recount atoms and state the relevant system boundary.

workedExample.prompt: Balance Mg + O₂ → MgO without changing the formulas.
steps: The left side has two oxygen atoms; one MgO on the right has only one.
Place 2 before MgO to give two oxygen atoms and two magnesium atoms on the right.
Place 2 before Mg: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
workedExample.conclusion: Both sides contain two magnesium atoms and two oxygen atoms. The equation gives a 2:1:2 amount ratio, not equal masses.

misconceptions.mistake: Changing O₂ into O to balance an equation.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the correct substance formula and adjust coefficients.

misconceptions.mistake: Claiming a gas-producing open reaction destroys mass.
misconceptions.correction: Include the escaped gas when accounting for the total mass.

practice.prompt: Balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O using the smallest whole-number coefficients.
hints: Make the oxygen counts match first.
solution: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
Both sides contain four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms.

practice.prompt: An open reaction vessel loses 1.2 g while a gas escapes. Explain why this observation alone does not contradict conservation of mass.
hints: What has crossed the measured system boundary?
solution: The balance measures the vessel and its remaining contents, not the escaped gas.
If 1.2 g of gas leaves and no other matter crosses the boundary, the total including that gas is unchanged.
A complete account must also consider splashing or other transfers before assigning all loss to gas.

practice.prompt: A learner sees bubbles after warming a liquid and concludes a new substance must have formed. Evaluate the conclusion and identify useful additional evidence.
hints: A physical change can also produce bubbles.
solution: Bubbles may indicate boiling or release of dissolved gas as well as a reaction.
Compare the conditions and identify whether the collected gas or remaining material is chemically different using an appropriate supervised test.
The observation alone is insufficient to establish chemical change.

practice.prompt: Balance N₂ + H₂ → NH₃ and check both element totals.
hints: Start with two nitrogen atoms.
Then count hydrogen in the product.
solution: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.
Both sides contain two nitrogen atoms and six hydrogen atoms.

practice.prompt: A learner changes CO₂ into CO to balance C + O₂ → CO₂. Explain the error and give the balanced original equation.
hints: The original product identity is fixed.
Count atoms before changing anything.
solution: C + O₂ → CO₂ is already balanced: one C and two O atoms on each side.
Changing CO₂ to CO specifies a different product and therefore a different reaction.

checklist: I account for matter crossing the boundary.

notes.title: Atom totals constrain coefficients
paragraphs: A balanced equation records atom conservation during a specified reaction. Coefficients multiply whole formulas; subscripts belong to the substance identity and cannot be adjusted just to make totals match. Polyatomic groups may be counted together when they remain unchanged on both sides, although the final check should still count each element. State symbols add information about physical states, while an arrow states a chemical transformation rather than an equality of masses per molecule. The equation’s ratios connect numbers of particles or moles. Converting these ratios into masses requires the appropriate molar masses.

workedExamples.prompt: Balance Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃ with the smallest whole-number coefficients.
steps: Choose 2Al₂O₃ to give six oxygen atoms, requiring 3O₂.
The two product units contain four aluminium atoms, so use 4Al.
workedExamples.conclusion: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃ conserves four Al and six O atoms.

flashcards.front: What can be changed when balancing?
flashcards.back: Coefficients before formulas.

flashcards.front: What does 3CO₂ contain?
flashcards.back: Three carbon atoms and six oxygen atoms.

flashcards.front: What do balanced coefficients compare?
flashcards.back: Particle numbers or mole amounts.

flashcards.front: What does changing a formula subscript do?
flashcards.back: It changes the specified substance or ion.

diagrams.title: Atom totals constrain coefficients
diagrams.description: Oxygen and aluminium counts must agree simultaneously.

lessons.summary: Use a balanced equation to relate amounts of reactants and products, including a simple limiting-reactant comparison.
objectives: Convert between mass and amount using molar mass.
Use coefficients as mole ratios.
Identify a limiting reactant from available amounts.
explanation: A mole is an amount of substance containing a fixed number of specified entities. Molar mass links amount and mass through n = m/M. The entities and units matter: one mole of oxygen molecules is not the same entity count as one mole of oxygen atoms. A balanced equation relates amounts in moles through its coefficients; it does not usually give the same numerical mass ratio.

For a reaction with more than one reactant, compare what each available amount could produce using the equation. The reactant allowing the smaller product amount is limiting under the assumed complete reaction. Theoretical yield follows from this ideal accounting. An actual isolated mass may be smaller because of incomplete reaction or collection losses, and can appear larger if the collected material contains impurities or solvent.
keyIdeas: Convert mass to moles before using a mole ratio.
A coefficient multiplies the amount of the specified substance.
Yield calculations need assumptions about purity and completeness.

definitions.meaning: An amount containing 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified entities.
Mass per mole of a specified substance, commonly in g/mol.
The reactant that restricts the theoretical product amount in the stated reaction.

method: Balance the equation and identify the requested substance.
Convert given masses to amounts with consistent molar-mass units.
Apply the coefficient ratio and check for a limiting reactant.
Convert to the requested units and state the ideal-yield assumptions.

workedExample.prompt: In the equation CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, calculate the theoretical mass of CO₂ from 10.0 g pure CaCO₃. Use molar masses 100 g/mol and 44 g/mol respectively and assume complete conversion.
steps: Amount of CaCO₃ = 10.0/100 = 0.100 mol.
The equation gives one mole of CO₂ per mole of CaCO₃, so CO₂ amount = 0.100 mol.
workedExample.conclusion: The theoretical carbon dioxide mass is 4.40 g under the stated assumptions. This calculation is an amount balance, not a practical reaction procedure.

misconceptions.mistake: Applying the coefficient ratio directly to masses.
misconceptions.correction: Convert to moles, use the ratio, then convert back with the relevant molar mass.

misconceptions.mistake: Selecting the limiting reactant by whichever mass is smaller.
misconceptions.correction: Compare available amounts against their equation coefficients.

practice.prompt: Find the amount in 9.0 g of water using molar mass 18 g/mol.
hints: Use n = m/M.
solution: n = 9.0/18 = 0.50 mol of water molecules.

practice.prompt: For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 3 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂ are available. Assuming complete reaction, find the limiting reactant, water amount and unused hydrogen amount.
hints: Compare available amount divided by its coefficient.
solution: Hydrogen permits 3/2 = 1.5 reaction units; oxygen permits 1/1 = 1.
Oxygen limits the reaction, producing 2 mol water and using 2 mol hydrogen.
Unused hydrogen = 3 - 2 = 1 mol.

practice.prompt: A calculation predicts 5.0 g of pure product. Only 4.0 g is collected. Find percentage yield and give two distinct possible reasons for the shortfall.
hints: Compare actual with theoretical mass.
solution: Percentage yield = 4.0/5.0 × 100% = 80%.
Incomplete reaction could reduce product formation; transfer or separation losses could reduce the amount collected.
The mass alone does not identify which cause occurred.

practice.prompt: Find the solute amount in 250 mL of a 0.40 mol/L solution.
hints: Convert mL to L.
Use n = cV.

practice.prompt: A solution containing 0.060 mol solute has final volume 0.300 L. What volume would give 0.10 mol/L if diluted without loss?
hints: Amount remains fixed.
Rearrange c = n/V.
solution: Required final volume = 0.060/0.10 = 0.600 L.
The volume must increase by 0.300 L, assuming additive solution volumes for the classroom calculation.
successCriteria: Distinguishes final volume from added volume.

checklist: I distinguish theoretical formation from collection.

notes.title: Dilution conserves solute
paragraphs: A solution’s molar concentration relates amount of solute to solution volume: c = n/V. Volume must be expressed in units compatible with the concentration, commonly litres for mol/L. Dilution adds solvent while retaining the solute amount if none reacts or is lost. Consequently c₁V₁ = c₂V₂ for the same solute, but this relationship does not describe a reaction that consumes it. When reactions occur, first determine each reactant amount and use the balanced equation. A smaller solution volume is not automatically a smaller amount because concentrations may differ.

workedExamples.prompt: A 0.20 mol/L solution occupies 0.150 L. It is diluted to 0.600 L without loss. Find solute amount and final concentration.
steps: Initial amount = 0.20 × 0.150 = 0.030 mol.
Final concentration = 0.030/0.600 = 0.050 mol/L.
workedExamples.conclusion: Volume quadruples while concentration falls to one-quarter; solute amount is conserved.

flashcards.front: What is c = n/V?
flashcards.back: Concentration equals solute amount divided by solution volume.

flashcards.front: How many litres are 250 mL?
What is conserved in ideal dilution?
flashcards.back: The amount of solute.

flashcards.front: Can dilution ratios replace reaction stoichiometry?
flashcards.back: No; reacting solutes require an amount balance.

diagrams.title: Dilution conserves solute
diagrams.description: The same amount is distributed through a larger solution volume.

edges.label: divide conserved amount by new volume

lessons.summary: Explain acid-base behaviour using particles and distinguish strength, concentration and measured pH.
objectives: Describe acids and bases using proton transfer.
Distinguish strong from concentrated.
Interpret simple pH comparisons and neutralisation.
explanation: In the proton-transfer model, an acid donates a proton and a base accepts one. In water, acids increase hydronium ion concentration; the shorter notation H⁺ is often used for the hydrated proton. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water to produce hydroxide ions. Neutralisation between a simple acid and hydroxide involves these ions forming water, while the other ions can form a salt.

Strength describes the extent of ionisation or reaction with water, whereas concentration describes how much solute is present in a given volume. A dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid are therefore possible. pH is a logarithmic measure related to hydrogen-ion activity; in a dilute classroom approximation, a one-unit decrease represents ten times the hydrogen-ion concentration. Neutral pH is approximately seven at 25°C, with its exact value depending on temperature.
keyIdeas: Strength and concentration answer different questions.
A lower pH represents greater hydrogen-ion activity.
Neutralisation does not always make the final mixture neutral.

definitions.meaning: A proton donor in the Brønsted-Lowry model.
A proton acceptor in the Brønsted-Lowry model.
A base that dissolves in water and produces hydroxide ions.

method: Identify the acid, base and relevant ions.
Separate statements about strength from concentration.
Use pH comparisons with the stated temperature and dilute-solution approximation.
Check reactant amounts and excess before predicting the final mixture.

workedExample.prompt: Two dilute aqueous solutions at the same temperature have pH 3 and pH 5. Compare hydrogen-ion concentrations using the classroom approximation.
steps: The pH difference is 5 - 3 = 2 units.
Each unit corresponds to a factor of ten in the inverse direction.
The pH 3 solution has 10² = 100 times the hydrogen-ion concentration.
workedExample.conclusion: The comparison is 100 times, not twice. These pH values alone do not establish the acids’ intrinsic strengths or the amounts needed for complete neutralisation.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling every low-concentration acid weak.
misconceptions.correction: Dilute describes concentration; weak describes partial ionisation under stated conditions.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming any mixture of acid and alkali finishes at pH 7.
misconceptions.correction: Excess reactant and the acid-base system affect the final pH.

practice.prompt: For dilute aqueous solutions, compare hydrogen-ion concentrations at pH 4 and pH 6.
hints: Use a factor of ten per pH unit.
solution: The pH 4 solution has 10² = 100 times the hydrogen-ion concentration of the pH 6 solution.

practice.prompt: Explain how an acid can be strong and dilute at the same time.
hints: Separate extent of ionisation from amount per volume.
solution: Strong means the acid is essentially fully ionised in the stated aqueous conditions.
Dilute means there is a relatively small amount of acid per unit volume.
The two descriptions concern different properties and are compatible.

practice.prompt: An idealised mixture initially contains 0.03 mol H⁺ and 0.02 mol OH⁻. Using H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, find the excess ion amount and say whether an exact final pH can be found without volume information.
hints: The ion ratio is one to one.
solution: 0.02 mol of each ion reacts, leaving 0.01 mol H⁺ in excess.
The simple model predicts an acidic mixture.
An exact pH needs the final volume and appropriate solution assumptions.

practice.prompt: A mixture has 0.008 mol H⁺ and 0.006 mol OH⁻. Find excess ions after complete neutralisation.
hints: Use a 1:1 ratio.
Subtract the smaller amount.
solution: 0.006 mol of each ion reacts.
0.002 mol H⁺ remains, so the simple model predicts an acidic mixture.

practice.prompt: Two acid solutions have the same pH. Does this alone prove they have the same total amount of acid available for neutralisation?
hints: Volume is not supplied.
pH concerns hydrogen-ion activity, not total acid inventory.
solution: The solutions could have different volumes, giving different total amounts even with equal concentration.
Acid dissociation and concentration also matter; equal pH alone does not establish equal neutralisation capacity.

checklist: I avoid predicting exact pH without enough information.

notes.title: Account for neutralisation and excess
paragraphs: Neutralisation involves proton transfer, and the net ionic equation for a strong aqueous acid with hydroxide is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. The remaining ions must still be accounted for even when omitted from that equation. Equal volumes do not ensure complete neutralisation: concentrations and the number of protons or hydroxide ions involved determine the amount ratio. At introductory level, a strong monoprotic acid and a strong hydroxide base react in a one-to-one ion ratio. After reaction, excess acid or base controls the simple prediction; exact pH also requires volume and a stated solution model.

workedExamples.prompt: An ideal mixture contains 0.015 mol H⁺ and 0.020 mol OH⁻. Determine the excess ion and water formed by neutralisation.
steps: The 1:1 reaction consumes all 0.015 mol H⁺ and 0.015 mol OH⁻.
OH⁻ remaining = 0.020 − 0.015 = 0.005 mol; 0.015 mol water forms.
workedExamples.conclusion: The model leaves excess hydroxide, so the mixture is basic.

flashcards.front: What is the hydroxide neutralisation ratio?
flashcards.back: One H⁺ reacts with one OH⁻.

flashcards.front: Do equal volumes imply equal reacting amounts?
flashcards.back: No; concentration and stoichiometry matter.

flashcards.front: What are spectator ions?
flashcards.back: Ions unchanged by the net ionic reaction.

flashcards.front: What does excess hydroxide suggest?
flashcards.back: A basic final solution in this simple aqueous model.

diagrams.title: Account for neutralisation and excess
diagrams.description: The smaller reacting amount limits the one-to-one reaction.

lessons.summary: Account for energy transfer during chemical change and connect temperature measurements to a stated system.
objectives: Distinguish exothermic from endothermic changes.
Explain the energy costs of breaking and making bonds.
Estimate heat transfer using supplied calorimetry data.
explanation: Choose the reacting substances as the chemical system. An exothermic change transfers energy from that system to the surroundings; an endothermic change takes energy in. Under suitable constant-pressure conditions, a negative enthalpy change describes an exothermic reaction. A rising solution temperature can be evidence of released energy, but interpreting it requires an account of what is being measured and other possible energy transfers.

Breaking a bond requires energy and forming a bond releases energy. The overall change depends on the balance of all bonds broken and formed, not on a claim that energy simply comes out of breaking bonds. A simple calorimetry model uses q = mcΔT for the heated material. Heat absorbed by the container or lost to the room makes that model incomplete unless those transfers are included.
keyIdeas: System and surroundings exchange energy.
Bond breaking and bond formation have opposite energy directions.
Measured temperature change is not itself a reaction enthalpy.

definitions.meaning: Describing a change that transfers energy from the chemical system to its surroundings.
Describing a change that absorbs energy into the chemical system from its surroundings.
The energy barrier that reacting particles must overcome along a reaction pathway.

method: Define the chemical system and measured surroundings.
Identify the sign of the energy transfer.
Use supplied masses, heat capacities and temperature changes consistently.
State neglected transfers and distinguish total heat from energy per mole.

workedExample.prompt: A classroom calorimetry record shows 100 g of solution warming by 5.0°C. Use c = 4.2 J/(g °C), neglect other heat transfers and estimate energy gained by the solution and lost by the reaction.
steps: q_solution = mcΔT = 100 × 4.2 × 5.0 = 2100 J.
The solution gains 2100 J.
With the stated assumptions, q_reaction = -2100 J.
workedExample.conclusion: The reaction is exothermic in this model. Energy per mole cannot be calculated without the reacted amount, and container heating or losses would require a fuller balance.

misconceptions.mistake: Saying breaking chemical bonds releases energy.
misconceptions.correction: Bond breaking requires energy; formation releases it. Compare both totals.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling a temperature rise of 5°C an energy of 5 J.
misconceptions.correction: Energy depends on mass and heat capacity as well as temperature change.

practice.prompt: A reaction absorbs 250 J from its surroundings. Classify the change and state the sign of the reaction’s energy gain.
hints: Focus on energy entering the chemical system.
solution: The change is endothermic.
The reaction system gains +250 J.

practice.prompt: A 50 g solution with c = 4.0 J/(g °C) warms from 20°C to 26°C. Neglect other transfers. Find its energy gain and the reaction’s energy change.
hints: First calculate the temperature difference.
solution: q_reaction = -1200 J under the stated assumptions.

practice.prompt: A simplified bond-energy account requires 900 kJ to break bonds and releases 1100 kJ when new bonds form. Find the net change and explain why a reaction can still need an initial energy input.
hints: Use energy required minus energy released.
solution: Net change = 900 - 1100 = -200 kJ, so the overall change is exothermic.
The reaction can still have an activation-energy barrier that must be overcome before the lower-energy products form.

practice.prompt: Reactants are at 25 kJ and products at 70 kJ for a stated amount. Find the reaction energy change and classify it.
hints: Subtract initial from final energy.
Positive change means the system gains energy.
solution: The reaction is endothermic for this energy account.

practice.prompt: A catalyst lowers a pathway peak from 100 to 65 kJ while reactants remain at 20 kJ and products at 5 kJ. Find both activation energies and explain the unchanged net change.
hints: Subtract the reactant level from each peak.
Compare product and reactant levels separately.
solution: Activation energies are 80 kJ and 45 kJ.
Net change remains 5 − 20 = −15 kJ because the endpoint energies are unchanged.

checklist: I distinguish bond breaking and formation.

notes.title: Energy levels show barrier and net change
paragraphs: A reaction energy diagram compares the energy of reactants and products while also showing an activation barrier. In an exothermic reaction, products have lower energy than reactants; the difference is transferred to the surroundings. The activation energy is measured upward from the reactant level to the transition-state peak, not from zero on the page. A catalyst offers an alternative pathway with a lower barrier. It does not change the reactant or product energy levels, so it changes rate rather than the net energy difference between the specified initial and final states.

workedExamples.prompt: A diagram gives reactants at 40 kJ, peak at 130 kJ and products at 10 kJ for a stated reaction amount. Find activation energy and reaction energy change.
steps: Forward activation energy = 130 − 40 = 90 kJ.
Reaction change = 10 − 40 = −30 kJ.
workedExamples.conclusion: The reaction is exothermic; a 90 kJ barrier still separates reactants from the peak.

flashcards.front: Where is forward activation energy measured from?
flashcards.back: Reactant energy to the pathway peak.

flashcards.front: What sign describes exothermic reaction energy?
flashcards.back: Negative for the reacting system.

flashcards.front: Does a catalyst change reaction energy difference?
flashcards.back: No, for the same initial and final states.

flashcards.front: Why can an exothermic reaction need starting energy?
flashcards.back: It still has an activation barrier.

diagrams.title: Energy levels show barrier and net change
diagrams.description: The rise to the peak differs from the overall fall.

lessons.summary: Describe reaction rate from observations and use collision ideas without confusing faster change with greater final yield.
objectives: Calculate an average rate from a change and time interval.
Explain temperature and surface-area effects.
Distinguish rate from the final amount of product.
explanation: Reaction rate describes how quickly a reactant is consumed or a product is formed. A measured signal such as gas volume is useful only when it tracks the intended change under consistent conditions. Average rate uses a change over a finite time interval. Instantaneous rate is represented by the gradient of a tangent at a chosen time, so one overall average does not describe every stage of a slowing reaction.

In a simple collision model, particles must meet with sufficient energy and an appropriate arrangement to react. Raising temperature generally increases the fraction able to overcome the activation barrier. Increasing the exposed area of a solid can give more accessible reaction sites. A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower barrier; it changes rate but does not automatically increase the equilibrium product amount.
keyIdeas: Rate includes a time unit.
The measurement must track the reaction consistently.
A faster reaction need not form more product in the end.

definitions.meaning: Change in a measured reaction quantity divided by the corresponding elapsed time.
A substance that increases reaction rate through an alternative pathway and is regenerated overall.
A model relating reaction events to suitably arranged collisions with enough energy.

method: Identify the signal and explain what chemical change it tracks.
Choose the time interval or tangent appropriate to the question.
Calculate a change divided by time with units.
Explain a rate difference while keeping reactant amounts and conditions in view.

workedExample.prompt: A supplied record shows gas volume rising from 10 cm³ at 5 s to 34 cm³ at 17 s. Find the average production rate over this interval.
steps: Volume change = 34 - 10 = 24 cm³.
Time interval = 17 - 5 = 12 s.
Average rate = 24/12 = 2.0 cm³/s.
workedExample.conclusion: The average rate is 2.0 cm³/s for this interval. It is not necessarily the initial rate or the rate at 17 s.

misconceptions.mistake: Dividing the final reading by time when the initial reading is not zero.
misconceptions.correction: Use changes in both measured quantity and time.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming a catalyst adds extra reactant or shifts equilibrium.
misconceptions.correction: It affects the pathway and rates; unchanged conditions have the same equilibrium composition.

practice.prompt: A product volume increases by 45 cm³ in 15 s. Find the average rate.
hints: Divide the change by elapsed time.
solution: Average rate = 45/15 = 3.0 cm³/s.

practice.prompt: Equal masses of the same solid react under otherwise identical suitable conditions. Explain why smaller pieces may react faster and whether they must produce more product after complete reaction.
hints: Distinguish exposed area from total amount.
solution: Smaller pieces expose a larger total surface area, allowing more reaction sites to contact the other reactant.
The solid amount is unchanged, so the final theoretical product amount need not increase.
The conclusion assumes the same composition, limiting-reactant conditions and complete reaction.

practice.prompt: A graph of cumulative product amount becomes less steep and finally horizontal. Interpret both changes and give two possible reasons for the plateau.
hints: The slope represents production rate.
solution: Decreasing steepness means the production rate falls; a horizontal section means no measurable net increase.
A limiting reactant may have been consumed, or a reversible system may have reached equilibrium.
The graph alone does not distinguish those explanations.

practice.prompt: Cumulative gas readings are 12 cm³ at 4 s and 42 cm³ at 19 s. Find average rate over that interval.
hints: Use changes in both volume and time.
Do not divide final volume by final time.
solution: ΔV = 30 cm³; Δt = 15 s.
Average rate = 30/15 = 2.0 cm³/s.

practice.prompt: Two reactions with equal initial reactant amounts reach the same final gas volume, but one reaches it sooner. Interpret rate and yield.
hints: Compare the time needed for the same amount.
Separate completion amount from speed.
solution: The faster reaction produces the same final gas amount in less time.
Its rate is greater over relevant intervals, but the equal final volumes give no evidence of a greater gas yield.

checklist: I use changes rather than final readings alone.
I separate rate from final yield.

notes.title: Temperature affects successful collisions
paragraphs: Temperature affects collision frequency and the distribution of particle energies. A higher temperature generally increases the fraction of collisions with enough energy to overcome the activation barrier, which can strongly increase reaction rate. A catalyst instead provides an alternative pathway with a lower barrier. Neither explanation requires claiming that particles acquire new chemical identities before they react. Rate data must distinguish an initial slope from an average over a long interval. Comparing total product after a short fixed time can reveal rate differences, but it does not necessarily establish different final yields after completion.

workedExamples.prompt: Two hypothetical reactions produce 18 cm³ and 30 cm³ gas during their first 10 s under matched collection conditions. Compare average initial-interval rates.
steps: Rate A = 18/10 = 1.8 cm³/s; rate B = 30/10 = 3.0 cm³/s.
workedExamples.conclusion: B’s average rate is about 1.67 times A’s over this interval; final yields remain unknown.

flashcards.front: How can temperature increase reaction rate?
flashcards.back: It raises the fraction of collisions exceeding the activation barrier.

flashcards.front: How does a catalyst change the pathway?
flashcards.back: It provides a lower activation barrier.

flashcards.front: What does a graph tangent estimate?
flashcards.back: Instantaneous rate at that point.

flashcards.front: Does more product after 10 s prove a greater final yield?
flashcards.back: No; it may reflect a faster reaction.

diagrams.title: Temperature affects successful collisions
diagrams.description: Rate depends on more than counting collisions alone.

nodes.label: Higher temperature
nodes.detail: Particles have a changed energy distribution

lessons.summary: Explain dynamic equilibrium and reason about a simple change without treating equilibrium as a stopped reaction.
objectives: Describe equal forward and reverse rates.
Distinguish constant concentrations from equal concentrations.
Explain a catalyst’s effect on reaching equilibrium.
explanation: A reversible reaction can proceed in both directions. In a closed system at fixed conditions, it can reach dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse reaction rates become equal while both processes continue. The amounts of reactants and products then remain constant on the macroscopic scale. Equal rates do not mean equal concentrations, and constant concentration alone does not prove equilibrium without information about the process.

If conditions change, the old balance may no longer hold. A simple qualitative response can often be predicted by considering which direction reduces the imposed disturbance, while recognising that equilibrium is only partially shifted. A catalyst accelerates both directions through the alternative pathway and helps the system reach equilibrium sooner. At the same temperature and other conditions, it does not change the equilibrium composition.
keyIdeas: Equilibrium remains active at the particle level.
Equal rates are different from equal amounts.
A disturbance and the subsequent response are separate events.

definitions.meaning: A reaction that can proceed from reactants to products and in the reverse direction.
A state where forward and reverse rates are equal and macroscopic composition stays constant at fixed conditions.
A system that exchanges no matter with its surroundings, though energy exchange may occur.

method: Identify the reversible change and whether matter can escape.
Describe the initial balance in terms of rates.
State the disturbance and the direction that partly opposes it.
Separate the final composition from the speed of reaching it.

workedExample.prompt: For the idealised reversible change A ⇌ B at equilibrium, explain what follows when extra A is added at unchanged temperature and volume.
steps: Adding A immediately raises its concentration and disturbs the previous balance.
The net reaction proceeds towards B as the forward and reverse rates readjust.
A new equilibrium is reached with equal rates; not all A must disappear.
workedExample.conclusion: The system shifts towards B under the stated simple model. This predicts a direction, not the final amounts without additional equilibrium information.

misconceptions.mistake: Saying both reactions stop at equilibrium.
misconceptions.correction: Forward and reverse events continue at equal rates.

misconceptions.mistake: Saying a catalyst increases the equilibrium yield.
misconceptions.correction: It changes how quickly equilibrium is reached, not its composition at the same conditions.

practice.prompt: At equilibrium a mixture contains more B than A. Is this inconsistent with equal forward and reverse rates?
hints: Amounts and rates are different quantities.
solution: No. Equal forward and reverse rates can occur with unequal amounts or concentrations.
Equilibrium requires constant macroscopic composition, not equal amounts of every substance.

practice.prompt: For A ⇌ B in a closed system at equilibrium, some B is removed while temperature and volume stay constant. Predict the subsequent net direction and qualify the prediction.
hints: Which direction replaces some of the removed B?
solution: The net change proceeds towards B under the simple equilibrium model.
A new balance is established as forward and reverse rates become equal again.
This does not imply complete conversion of A or exact replacement of all removed B.

practice.prompt: A learner adds a catalyst to increase the final equilibrium fraction of product at unchanged temperature. Evaluate the plan.
hints: Consider both directions of the reversible change.
solution: A catalyst speeds the forward and reverse pathways and can shorten the time to equilibrium.
It does not change the final equilibrium fraction at the same conditions.
More product at an early measurement time would not establish a changed equilibrium yield.

practice.prompt: For X(g) ⇌ 2Y(g), predict the equilibrium shift on expansion at unchanged temperature.
hints: Expansion lowers pressure.
Compare gas particle counts.
solution: Lower pressure favours the side with more gas particles.
The net shift is towards Y, which has two particles per reaction unit rather than one.

practice.prompt: For A(g) + B(g) ⇌ C(g) + D(g), explain why the simple particle-count rule predicts no pressure-driven composition shift on compression.
hints: Count total gas coefficients on each side.
Both sides respond with the same particle-number factor.
solution: Each side has two gas particles per reaction unit.
Neither side has fewer gas particles, so compression gives no preferred direction under this idealised rule.

checklist: I compare rates rather than demanding equal amounts.
I distinguish speed from equilibrium composition.

notes.title: Compression can change gas composition
paragraphs: Dynamic equilibrium requires opposing processes to continue at equal rates within a suitable closed system. Amounts can be constant even though particles keep reacting. For gas equilibria, compression may change the equilibrium composition when the two sides contain different total numbers of gas particles. In the school model, increased pressure favours the side with fewer gaseous particles at constant temperature. Count coefficients of gases only, and do not turn this into a rule that pressure always increases product yield. The equation, physical states and direction of the pressure change determine the prediction.

workedExamples.prompt: For the ideal gas equilibrium A(g) + B(g) ⇌ C(g), predict the effect of compression at constant temperature.
steps: The left side has two moles of gas per reaction unit; the right has one.
Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas particles, giving a net shift towards C.
workedExamples.conclusion: Both forward and reverse processes continue at the new equilibrium.

flashcards.front: What is equal at dynamic equilibrium?
flashcards.back: Forward and reverse rates.

flashcards.front: Must equilibrium amounts be equal?
flashcards.back: No; constant amounts need not be equal.

flashcards.front: Which side is favoured by compression in the simple gas model?
flashcards.back: The side with fewer gaseous particles.

flashcards.front: Does a catalyst move equilibrium at fixed temperature?
flashcards.back: No; it speeds approach to equilibrium.

diagrams.title: Compression can change gas composition
diagrams.description: Particle counts determine this pressure response.

nodes.label: A(g) + B(g)
nodes.detail: Two gas particles per reaction unit

nodes.label: C(g) favoured
nodes.detail: One gas particle per reaction unit

lessons.summary: Read simple carbon structures and connect functional groups to classification without confusing formula with connectivity.
objectives: Identify simple alkane, alkene and alcohol structures.
Distinguish molecular and structural formulas.
Explain why isomers can have different properties.
explanation: Carbon commonly forms four covalent bonds and can join other carbon atoms into chains or rings. A molecular formula records the number of each kind of atom, but does not show how those atoms are connected. A structural formula gives that extra information. Two compounds can therefore share a molecular formula while having different connectivity and different physical or chemical properties.

Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Acyclic alkanes contain only single carbon-carbon bonds and follow CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Acyclic alkenes with one double bond follow CₙH₂ₙ, but that formula alone does not prove an alkene because ring structures can share it. An alcohol contains an appropriate hydroxyl group attached to a saturated carbon. Classification needs the structure and functional group, not merely an oxygen or carbon count.
keyIdeas: Connectivity adds information beyond atom counts.
General formulas require stated structural restrictions.
A functional group helps predict a family of chemical behaviour.

definitions.meaning: A compound containing only carbon and hydrogen.
An atom or group of atoms associated with characteristic chemical behaviour in a molecule.
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different atom connectivity.

method: Count atoms and check ordinary carbon valency.
Identify single and multiple bonds and any functional group.
Classify using the structure and applicable formula restrictions.
Distinguish what is known from a molecular formula alone.

workedExample.prompt: Compare CH₃CH₂OH and CH₃OCH₃. Count atoms and explain whether they represent the same structure.
steps: Both contain two carbon atoms, six hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom: C₂H₆O.
CH₃CH₂OH has a hydroxyl group on a saturated carbon and is an alcohol.
CH₃OCH₃ has oxygen between two carbon groups and is an ether.
workedExample.conclusion: They are structural isomers with different connectivity. The molecular formula alone does not select the functional group or guarantee identical properties.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming every compound containing carbon is a hydrocarbon.
misconceptions.correction: A hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen.

misconceptions.mistake: Using CₙH₂ₙ as proof of a carbon-carbon double bond.
misconceptions.correction: A saturated single-ring structure can share that formula; inspect connectivity.

practice.prompt: Find the molecular formula of an acyclic alkane with five carbon atoms.
hints: Use CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
solution: Hydrogen count = 2 × 5 + 2 = 12.
The formula is C₅H₁₂.

practice.prompt: Classify CH₃CH₃, CH₂=CH₂ and CH₃CH₂OH as alkane, alkene or alcohol, explaining the structural evidence.
hints: Inspect bonds and the hydroxyl group.
solution: CH₃CH₃ is an alkane with only single bonds between its carbons.
CH₂=CH₂ is an alkene with a carbon-carbon double bond.
CH₃CH₂OH is an alcohol with a hydroxyl group on a saturated carbon.

practice.prompt: A learner identifies an unknown C₃H₆ compound as an alkene using only its molecular formula. Explain why the identification is incomplete.
hints: Can a ring produce the same atom count?
solution: C₃H₆ fits the formula for an acyclic alkene with one double bond, such as propene.
It also fits a saturated ring structure, cyclopropane.
Structural evidence is required to distinguish these possibilities; atom counts alone are insufficient.

practice.prompt: An acyclic alkane has seven carbon atoms. Give its molecular formula and explain the hydrogen count.
hints: Use CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
Substitute n = 7.
solution: Hydrogen count = 2 × 7 + 2 = 16.
The molecular formula is C₇H₁₆ for the stated acyclic alkane.

practice.prompt: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH and CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ have the same formula. Identify their shared functional group and the structural difference.
hints: Locate OH along the chain.
Same atom totals do not require identical connectivity.
solution: Both contain an alcohol hydroxyl group and have formula C₃H₈O.
In the first OH is on an end carbon; in the second it is on the middle carbon, so they are structural isomers.

checklist: I state the general formula’s restrictions.
I distinguish formula evidence from structure evidence.

notes.title: Connectivity separates organic families
paragraphs: A homologous series groups organic compounds with a shared functional group and a regular pattern of composition. Alkanes contain only single carbon–carbon bonds in the acyclic school examples, while alkenes contain a carbon–carbon double bond. Alcohols contain a hydroxyl group bonded to carbon. A structural formula shows connectivity that a molecular formula alone can hide. For example, compounds with the same atom totals can arrange those atoms differently and therefore have different properties. When naming a simple compound, count the carbon chain and identify the functional group before choosing the ending.

workedExamples.prompt: Compare CH₃CH₂CH₃ and CH₃CH=CH₂ using atom counts and bonding.
steps: The first is C₃H₈ with only single carbon–carbon bonds: propane, an alkane.
The second is C₃H₆ with a carbon–carbon double bond: propene, an alkene.
workedExamples.conclusion: The double bond changes the series and hydrogen count.

flashcards.front: What feature defines an alkene?
flashcards.back: A carbon–carbon double bond.

flashcards.front: What functional group characterises an alcohol?
flashcards.back: A hydroxyl group attached to carbon.

flashcards.front: What does a structural formula reveal?
flashcards.back: How atoms are connected.

flashcards.front: What is the acyclic alkane formula?
flashcards.back: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

diagrams.title: Connectivity separates organic families
diagrams.description: Carbon count alone does not determine the family.

nodes.label: Three-carbon skeleton
nodes.detail: A chain of three carbon atoms

edges.label: complete with hydrogen for an alkane
introduce a double bond and two fewer hydrogens

lessons.summary: Connect chemical processes to environmental evidence while distinguishing concentration, exposure and causal claims.
objectives: Explain selected carbon and nutrient processes.
Calculate a concentration from mass and volume.
Evaluate a comparison using sampling context and limitations.
explanation: Environmental chemistry follows substances through air, water, soil and living systems. A concentration describes the amount of a substance in a quantity of material, not the total amount present everywhere. Comparing water samples therefore requires compatible units, sampling locations and timing. A concentration can fall through dilution while the total mass of the substance in the larger system remains unchanged.

Chemical mechanisms help explain environmental changes. Carbon dioxide can absorb infrared radiation and participate in Earth’s energy balance; this differs from the chemical processes that deplete stratospheric ozone. Excess nutrient input can support algal growth, with subsequent decomposition consuming dissolved oxygen under suitable conditions. A plausible mechanism matters, but attributing a particular observed change still requires evidence about sources, timing, other influences and measurement quality.
keyIdeas: A concentration needs both an amount and a denominator.
Dilution redistributes a substance rather than destroying it.
A mechanism supports investigation without proving a specific cause on its own.

definitions.meaning: The amount of a substance per specified quantity of mixture or solution.
Nutrient enrichment that can cause increased biological growth and subsequent oxygen depletion in a water body.
Oxygen present in solution in water and available to aquatic organisms.

method: Define the substance, environmental system and question.
Check sample units, locations, timing and comparison conditions.
Calculate the relevant amount or concentration.
Connect the evidence to a mechanism and identify alternative explanations.

workedExample.prompt: A hypothetical water sample contains 12 mg of a dissolved substance in 3 L. Pure water is added to make 6 L, with no substance removed or reacted. Find both concentrations.
steps: Initial concentration = 12/3 = 4 mg/L.
Final mass remains 12 mg while volume becomes 6 L.
Final concentration = 12/6 = 2 mg/L.
workedExample.conclusion: The concentration halves, but the substance’s total mass remains 12 mg. This arithmetic does not establish whether either sample meets a health or environmental standard.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating a lower concentration after dilution as proof of removal.
misconceptions.correction: Check the total mass as well as the volume.

misconceptions.mistake: Using greenhouse warming and ozone depletion as interchangeable explanations.
misconceptions.correction: They involve different processes even when some substances influence both.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical sample contains 8 mg of solute in 2 L. Calculate its concentration.
hints: Use mass divided by volume.
solution: Concentration = 8/2 = 4 mg/L.

practice.prompt: Explain how an increased nutrient input can contribute to a later decrease in dissolved oxygen in a lake.
hints: Include growth, death and decomposition rather than saying nutrients directly remove oxygen.
solution: Additional nutrients can support greater algal growth when other conditions allow it.
When organisms die, decomposers break down organic matter and consume oxygen through respiration.
This can lower dissolved oxygen; the outcome depends on conditions such as mixing and replenishment.

practice.prompt: A downstream sample has a higher solute concentration than one upstream sample. Evaluate the claim that a nearby factory must be responsible.
hints: A single spatial comparison may have several explanations.
solution: The comparison identifies a difference but does not uniquely identify its source.
Repeat sampling at matched times, check flow and other inputs, and compare the relevant chemical signatures and discharge records where available.
Report measurement uncertainty and alternative sources before assigning responsibility.

practice.prompt: A steady stream has concentration 3 mg/L and flow 12 L/s. Find solute transport per second and over 10 s.
hints: Multiply concentration by flow.
Then multiply the rate by time.
solution: Rate = 3 × 12 = 36 mg/s.
Over 10 s, transported mass = 360 mg.

practice.prompt: After rain, measured concentration halves while river flow triples. Assuming representative steady readings, does solute transport fall?
hints: Compare products of concentration and flow.
Use the original transport rate as one unit.
solution: New transport = 0.5 × 3 = 1.5 times the original.
The load rate rises by 50%, despite lower concentration.

checklist: I track total mass and volume separately.
I connect the proposed mechanism to evidence.

notes.title: Concentration and flow determine load
paragraphs: Water-quality comparisons should distinguish concentration from pollutant load. Concentration gives amount per water volume, while load is the total amount transported over an interval or its rate of transport. A river with lower concentration can carry a larger load if its flow is much greater. In a simple steady-flow model, mass transport rate equals concentration multiplied by volume flow rate, provided units match and the concentration represents the flowing water. Removing a fraction of a pollutant can reduce load, but an environmental judgement also needs the substance identity, exposure, persistence and relevant ecological context.

workedExamples.prompt: Stream A carries 2 mg/L solute at 30 L/s; stream B carries 5 mg/L at 8 L/s. Compare transport rates.
workedExamples.conclusion: A has the lower concentration but the larger solute transport rate.

flashcards.front: What is concentration?
flashcards.back: Amount of substance per volume of solution.

flashcards.front: How is steady solute transport rate calculated?
flashcards.back: Concentration multiplied by volume flow rate.

flashcards.front: Can lower concentration mean greater load?
flashcards.back: Yes, when volume flow is sufficiently larger.

flashcards.front: What information is needed beyond solute amount?
flashcards.back: Substance identity and relevant exposure or ecological effects.

diagrams.title: Concentration and flow determine load
diagrams.description: A larger water flow can outweigh a lower concentration.

edges.label: cancel litres to obtain mass per second

lessons.summary: Design a clear classroom chemistry comparison with measured variables, repeatable observations and documented limitations.
objectives: Operationally define a measured outcome.
Distinguish repeated measurements from controlled variables.
Propose improvements linked to a specific source of uncertainty.
explanation: A useful experimental plan states a question that the measurements can actually answer. Define the independent variable, the response and the relevant controls. For a dissolving-time comparison, for example, “fully dissolved” needs an observation rule; otherwise different observers may stop timing at different points. The procedure also needs a clear start point and consistent sample preparation.

Keep all raw observations alongside any calculated mean. Repeats estimate variation but cannot repair a shared calibration error or an inconsistent definition. Select equipment and quantities within an established teacher-approved procedure and document the relevant handling and disposal arrangements. Evaluation should connect each limitation to its likely effect and a practical improvement, rather than listing generic statements about human error.
keyIdeas: An operational definition makes a judgement repeatable.
Controls should address plausible competing influences.
A useful improvement targets a named limitation.

definitions.meaning: A precise description of how a variable or endpoint will be observed or measured.
A further observation under the same intended conditions to examine variation.
A consistent or predictably varying measurement bias that repeats alone do not remove.

method: State a measurable question and endpoint.
Specify the changed variable, measured response and relevant controls.
Plan repeats and a table that preserves raw readings and units.
Link limitations to improvements within the approved classroom procedure.

workedExample.prompt: Outline a classroom comparison of how stirring affects the time for a fixed small amount of sugar to dissolve in room-temperature water.
steps: Change a defined stirring condition and measure time from adding sugar to a specified no-visible-crystals endpoint.
Keep sugar mass and grain size, water volume, temperature and container consistent.
Repeat each condition and record all times, including endpoint difficulties.
Use the same observation rule and compare timing spread before claiming a difference.
workedExample.conclusion: The plan tests a defined dissolving-time response. It does not by itself measure equilibrium solubility, and observer judgement remains a limitation to evaluate.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling a faster dissolving time greater solubility.
misconceptions.correction: Rate describes how quickly dissolution occurs; solubility concerns the equilibrium amount at stated conditions.

misconceptions.mistake: Writing “human error” without a mechanism.
misconceptions.correction: Name the timing, reading or handling effect and explain how it influences the result.

practice.prompt: In a study of stirring condition and sugar dissolving time, identify the independent variable, dependent variable and one control.
hints: Distinguish the changed condition from the timed response.
solution: Independent variable: the defined stirring condition.
Dependent variable: time to the defined dissolving endpoint.
One control is the sugar mass, water volume or water temperature.

practice.prompt: Two observers use different meanings of “fully dissolved”. Explain the problem and propose a specific improvement.
hints: The endpoint itself is inconsistent.
solution: Different endpoint rules can produce different times even for identical physical behaviour.
Agree a visible-crystal endpoint and viewing conditions before collecting results, and use a consistent observer or checked recording method.
Repeats should then assess remaining variation rather than average incompatible definitions.

practice.prompt: A group changes stirring speed and water temperature together, then attributes a shorter dissolving time only to stirring. Evaluate the conclusion and redesign the comparison conceptually.
hints: More than one plausible influence changed.
solution: The comparison confounds stirring and temperature, so it cannot isolate stirring’s effect.
Compare stirring conditions while holding temperature and other relevant factors consistent; investigate temperature separately if needed.
Use repeated measurements and the same endpoint rule for each condition.

practice.prompt: Trial A uses “first colour seen” while trial B uses “strong permanent colour”. Why can their times not directly isolate the treatment effect?
hints: Compare the stopping rules.
A later threshold can itself produce a longer time.
solution: Different endpoints measure different stages of colour development.
Use one shared criterion before interpreting time differences as treatment effects.

practice.prompt: All low-concentration trials occur first and high-concentration trials later while room temperature rises. Identify the confound and an improved plan.
hints: Temperature can affect the response.
Separate treatment order from warming.
solution: Concentration and temperature change together, so the treatment effect is not isolated.
Control temperature and randomise trial order across independent preparations.

checklist: My improvement addresses a specific limitation.

notes.title: Endpoint definition controls measurement
paragraphs: A useful chemical comparison defines both the changed condition and a reproducible endpoint. When a visible colour change marks an endpoint, lighting, observer judgement and the chosen threshold can add variation. A reference standard or consistent instrument criterion can reduce ambiguity. Randomising trial order helps prevent slow changes in room conditions or equipment from aligning with one treatment. Independent repeats estimate variation between preparations; repeated readings of one prepared sample address a different question. Record unexpected results and investigate documented causes rather than discarding inconvenient values solely because they differ from the expected pattern.

workedExamples.prompt: A teacher-approved comparison measures colour-change time at two dilution levels. Plan how to reduce observer and order effects.
steps: Use the same stated colour reference or instrument threshold for every trial.
Randomise the order of independently prepared dilution trials while holding lighting and measurement conditions constant.
workedExamples.conclusion: These choices reduce interpretation and order biases without guaranteeing error-free data.

flashcards.front: What is an operational endpoint?
flashcards.back: A specified observable criterion for deciding when measurement stops.

flashcards.front: Why randomise trial order?
flashcards.back: To avoid aligning treatment with time-dependent changes.

flashcards.front: What does an independent repeat require?
flashcards.back: A separately prepared experimental unit or trial.

flashcards.front: Why retain unusual readings?
flashcards.back: They may reveal real variation or a documented procedural problem.

diagrams.title: Endpoint definition controls measurement
diagrams.description: A colour observation becomes comparable only with a consistent criterion.

lessons.summary: Interpret chemical measurements using units, variation and an explicit model rather than selecting only confirming results.
objectives: Summarise repeated chemical measurements without hiding spread.
Compare actual observations with a theoretical value.
Distinguish evidence of disagreement from an identified cause.
explanation: Start by asking what the measurement represents: mass of collected material, solution concentration or a signal used as a proxy. Preserve the original units and conditions before calculating a summary. A mean of repeats can be useful, but a small spread does not rule out contamination or calibration bias affecting every repeat. Compare like quantities and report enough information to see both centre and variation.

Theoretical values depend on assumptions such as purity, complete conversion and no transfer losses. A discrepancy tells you that observation and model differ under the stated account; it does not uniquely identify the reason. An apparent yield above 100% can indicate retained solvent or impurities, or an incorrect theoretical calculation. Unexpected results should trigger a documented check of assumptions and measurements, not automatic deletion or invented agreement.
keyIdeas: Know what the measured signal represents.
A mean can hide spread and shared bias.
A discrepancy needs investigation before causal attribution.

definitions.meaning: The product amount predicted from a balanced equation and stated ideal assumptions.
Actual product amount divided by theoretical product amount, multiplied by 100%.
An observation that differs noticeably from a pattern and needs investigation, not automatic exclusion.

method: Check what was measured, including units and sample condition.
Summarise repeats and report their spread.
Compare with a theoretical value using consistent quantities.
Investigate assumptions and possible causes while retaining the original evidence.

workedExample.prompt: A theoretical product mass is 2.00 g. Three collected masses are 1.72 g, 1.80 g and 1.88 g. Find the mean, range and percentage yield based on the mean.
steps: Mean-based percentage yield = 1.80/2.00 × 100% = 90%.
workedExample.conclusion: The mean-based yield is 90%, with a 0.16 g range in the collected masses. The data alone cannot separate incomplete reaction from collection loss or establish product purity.

misconceptions.mistake: Accepting a measured yield above 100% as proof of extra atoms being created.
misconceptions.correction: Check purity, retained liquid, mass readings and the theoretical calculation.

misconceptions.mistake: Removing a value because it lowers the reported yield.
misconceptions.correction: Exclude only with a documented, justified reason and report the decision transparently.

practice.prompt: Three masses are 3.2 g, 3.4 g and 3.3 g. Calculate their mean and range.
hints: Add all readings for the mean and compare the extremes for the range.

practice.prompt: A dry pure product should theoretically have mass 5.0 g, but a collected sample weighs 5.5 g. Calculate the apparent yield and explain why it cannot be accepted as the pure-product yield without further checks.
hints: The balance includes everything in the collected sample.
solution: Apparent yield = 5.5/5.0 × 100% = 110%.
Retained solvent or impurities could add mass; a weighing or theoretical-calculation error is also possible.
Check sample condition, purity and calculations before reporting a pure-product yield.

practice.prompt: Repeated measurements agree closely but all are below a model prediction. A learner concludes random variation is the only possible cause. Evaluate the claim.
hints: Agreement between repeats does not rule out shared effects.
solution: Close agreement indicates precision for these measurements, not necessarily accuracy or model validity.
A shared collection loss, calibration bias or an unsuitable model assumption could shift every result.
Use reference checks and a review of the procedure and assumptions to distinguish causes while retaining the readings.

practice.prompt: Calibration signal = 3c + 1 is valid from 0 to 8 mg/L. Find c for signal 16 and check the range.
hints: Subtract one first.
Divide the remainder by three.
solution: Five lies between zero and eight, so this is interpolation within the stated range.

practice.prompt: Standards cover 0–5 mg/L, but an unknown response gives a fitted estimate of 20 mg/L. Is the line alone sufficient to validate that result?
hints: Locate the estimate relative to standards.
Linearity was checked only over a limited range.
solution: Twenty mg/L lies well outside the calibration range, so the estimate is extrapolation.
Use a validated extended range or an appropriate teacher-approved dilution and correction before accepting the concentration.

notes.title: Convert instrument signal to concentration
paragraphs: A calibration relationship connects an instrument response to known standards. Within a validated linear range, the slope represents response per unit concentration and an intercept may account for a background signal. Subtract that background before converting an unknown response into concentration. Do not extrapolate far beyond the standards without checking that the relationship still holds. Closely repeated readings demonstrate repeatability, but an incorrect standard concentration or uncorrected instrument offset can shift every result. Report calculated concentrations with precision consistent with the measurements and retain the original readings so the calculation can be checked.

workedExamples.prompt: A supplied calibration is signal = 4c + 2 for c from 0 to 10 mg/L. An unknown has signal 22. Find c.
steps: Subtract background: 22 − 2 = 20.
Divide by slope: c = 20/4 = 5 mg/L.
workedExamples.conclusion: The result is within the stated calibration range.

flashcards.front: What does a calibration intercept represent in this model?
flashcards.back: The signal when concentration is zero.

flashcards.front: How is background corrected?
flashcards.back: Subtract the appropriate blank or intercept.

flashcards.front: What is extrapolation?
flashcards.back: Using the fitted relation outside its measured range.

flashcards.front: Can repeatable readings still be biased?
flashcards.back: Yes, a shared calibration error can shift them all.
